To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified novel monoclonal antibodies that inhibit HIV infection and cell fusion without affecting gp120 binding.
we have isolated two monoclonal antibodies that inhibit human immunodeficiency infection and syncytia formation but not binding of virus to cells.
two novel mAbs reactive with a region of CD4 distinct from the high affinity binding domain of the HIV envelope glycoprotein gp120 inhibit virus infection and fusion, but not virus binding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of anti-CD4 antibodies that inhibit HIV infection and syncytia formation.
the development of novel anti-HIV agents.
the molecular basis of the human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV) interaction with the cell surface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CD4 is not just a receptor for HIV but also a co-receptor for HIV.
the CD4 receptor has an active role in virus entry.
the CD4 molecule is a key component in the HIV life cycle, and that it has two distinct and separable functions: virus binding and membrane fusion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified two new mAbs, which inhibit HIV infection and cell fusion, but which do not inhibit virus binding to cells.
the third domain of the CD4 protein is critical for the fusion step, and the first domain of the CD-4 is critical for virus binding.
we have developed novel anti-CD4 mAbs that inhibit HIV infection and syncytial cell formation, but do not inhibit gp120 binding to CD4.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD4 is not just a receptor for HIV.
CD4 has two distinct roles in the HIV life cycle: one in virus binding and the other in membrane fusion.
CD4 is not just a passive target of HIV.
